title: High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions

concept.text: The innovation would be an integrated nuclear-powered spacecraft propulsion system that can deliver useful payloads through deep space over sustained missions, followed by enough successful operation to make the capability dependable and repeatable. Its defining achievement would be a working spacecraft and mission capability: a reactor, propulsion hardware and supporting systems that meet their performance and lifetime requirements together.

Two architectures fall within this concept. In nuclear thermal propulsion, reactor heat heats propellant that is expelled for thrust. In nuclear electric propulsion, reactor heat is converted into electricity that powers an electric thruster. The supplied technical evidence primarily concerns the electric route, including lithium-fed magnetoplasmadynamic plasma thrusters. These produce comparatively low, continuous thrust and can build up speed over time while using propellant efficiently; high electrical power does not by itself establish high thrust or a short journey.

For the electric route, the spacecraft must combine a sufficiently light and reliable reactor with power conversion, heat rejection, propulsion and their interfaces. Protection, shielding and controls must also fit the mission's mass and operating constraints. The central advance is making these systems work together for the required duration; separate reactor and thruster demonstrations establish only parts of that capability.

significance.text: A successful system could combine sustained propulsion, high propellant efficiency and an energy source that does not depend on strong sunlight. If the reactor, conversion equipment and thermal hardware are light and durable enough, this could reduce propellant and launch-mass burdens, support substantial payloads and make additional deep-space trajectories practical. These would be mission-level benefits: the mass saved in propellant must be assessed alongside the mass and operating demands of the nuclear propulsion system.

The revolutionary possibility is an expansion in practical mission scale and destinations. That possibility is conditional on the complete vehicle's mass, lifetime, power and thrust, and on the chosen trajectory. The reviewed conference paper explicitly treats propulsion selection as dependent on mission duration, habitat choices and operations. Neither electric propulsion's propellant efficiency nor a high-power ground test establishes that nuclear propulsion will outperform chemical propulsion on every mission, shorten every transit or lower total cost.

Downstream synthesis: dependable nuclear propulsion could support more ambitious robotic exploration and, with other advances, larger human expeditions. Routine human travel would additionally require adequate life support, crew protection, mission operations and affordable launch. Propulsion alone would therefore establish an enabling transportation capability, not routine human settlement or travel throughout the Solar System.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a flightworthy, integrated system that meets a useful deep-space mission's power, propulsion, mass and lifetime requirements simultaneously. Scaling a thruster or reactor separately does not resolve the spacecraft problem. For nuclear electric propulsion, reactor output must be converted into usable electricity, delivered to the thruster and accompanied by adequate heat rejection, with the combined equipment remaining within the vehicle's mass budget. The reviewed technical paper identifies subsystem power scaling and integrated system development as central challenges.

Endurance is a distinct barrier. A brief high-power test does not show that propulsion hardware can operate for the cumulative duration required by a mission. The reviewed conference paper identifies thruster lifetime as the largest gap between demonstrated performance and the requirement in its development context. A convincing system must sustain useful propulsion over the intended operating period while preserving the performance of its reactor, conversion equipment and thermal systems.

Engineering synthesis: shielding, protection and control requirements must be translated into a concrete spacecraft design, including their mass and effects on system operation. The supplied evidence does not provide a complete shielding or control specification, a universal acceptable system mass, or a numerical reliability threshold. Those requirements must be set for the selected payload, trajectory, operating duration and mission consequences.

The propulsion tradeoff also remains at mission scale. Electric thrusters conserve propellant by accelerating it efficiently, but their comparatively low thrust means that acceleration accumulates over time. Useful payload delivery therefore depends on the interaction of power, spacecraft mass, operating duration and trajectory. Demonstrating a power level alone leaves this mission-performance question open.

current_state.text: NASA's May 2, 2018 report describes the KRUSTY fission power experiment culminating in a 28-hour full-power ground test that simulated mission conditions. The prototype transferred reactor heat through passive sodium heat pipes to Stirling engines that generated electricity. This establishes a reported reactor-and-conversion ground demonstration. It does not establish an integrated propulsion flight, and a stated long-term design capability must not be read as evidence of a ten-year endurance test.

NASA's April 28, 2026 article reports that a lithium-fed magnetoplasmadynamic thruster reached input-power levels of up to 120 kilowatts during February 2026 testing in JPL's vacuum facility. This was a ground test of a propulsion component. The reported power level does not establish spacecraft performance, mission-duration endurance or operation with a reactor supplying the power. The article presents payload and launch-mass benefits as conditional on further development and nuclear integration.

The reviewed 19-page conference paper, IEPC-2024-841, supplies technical context on propulsion architecture, subsystem scaling and lifetime gaps. It is a development paper rather than evidence of a completed nuclear propulsion mission. Its discussion includes a statement attributed to a NASEM report; that report was encountered through the paper's quotation in the supplied review, rather than independently examined.

The retained NASA article dated October 20, 2026 describes SR-1 Freedom as a planned nuclear electric propulsion demonstration in deep space, with a planned 2028 launch. It describes integration of a fission reactor with a Brayton power conversion system. These are development plans, not a completed flight. October 20 is the article's date; the supplied review does not establish that the announcement event mentioned in the article occurred on that date.

The SR-1 article's retained version was updated November 6, 2026, after the November 1 assessment cutoff. The supplied record contains no independently recovered pre-cutoff version, so its exact wording and the availability of particular details by November 1 remain uncertain. The supplied review also contains no bounded freshness-search results establishing a comprehensive survey at that cutoff. These limits constrain conclusions about overall status; they do not negate the separately dated component reports.

Evidence boundary: the earlier research also mentioned historical nuclear thermal engine ground tests, but the supplied reviewed texts do not substantiate that historical assertion. It remains unverified within this record and cannot serve here as a documented milestone. This limitation does not establish that such tests did not occur, and it does not remove nuclear thermal propulsion from the concept's scope.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently measure a mission-duration deep-space flight of an integrated nuclear propulsion system delivering a useful payload on a trajectory that is impractical or substantially more burdensome using an available chemical alternative. Define the payload, destination or trajectory, operating duration and success conditions before evaluation. This is a proposed completion test, not an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Nuclear flight delivers payload on chemically impractical or burdensome trajectories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparison: specify the chemical alternative and the relevant measures of burden in advance, including launch mass, transit time and total mission cost where appropriate. Report the actual tradeoffs rather than requiring the nuclear system to win on every measure. The comparison should identify the conditions under which its advantage holds, including vehicle mass, power, propulsion duration and operational assumptions.
completion_criteria.label: Report chemical-alternative tradeoffs and conditions supporting the nuclear system’s advantage

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: provide independently assessable measurements of power delivered to propulsion, thrust and propellant consumption, achieved trajectory, delivered payload, cumulative operating time and degradation. Demonstrate reactor, conversion, thermal-management and propulsion operation together over the required mission duration. Report interruptions, failures and operating limits so that useful endurance can be distinguished from a short peak-power result.
completion_criteria.label: Measurements verify integrated propulsion operation over the required mission duration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed route to routine use: subsequent flights should establish repeatable payload delivery, reliability and actual operating costs under declared mission conditions. Independent reproduction or verification should be sufficient to test the principal performance claims. No particular repeat-flight count is established by the supplied evidence. A successful mission or finite series would demonstrate a bounded operating envelope; broader reliability and economic claims would require corresponding operational experience.
completion_criteria.label: Subsequent flights verify repeatable payload delivery, reliability and operating costs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NUC-10, Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites, has the closest overlap in dependable autonomous power and long operating life. NUC-04 adds spacecraft mass constraints, propulsion integration and trajectory performance. NUC-02, Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost, shares questions of manufacturability and cost, but inexpensive terrestrial electricity does not establish a sufficiently light space propulsion system. Each remains a distinct innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-06, Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure, and NUC-11, Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants, could contribute to reactor lifetime and thermal-system durability. NUC-09, Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention, overlaps with fuel endurance and containment. These are potential enabling advances; the supplied evidence does not establish that NUC-04 requires completion of any particular one of them.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-08, Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling, overlaps with dependable reactor protection and heat management. NUC-12, Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis, could support monitoring and control, but full three-dimensional diagnosis is not established here as a prerequisite for nuclear propulsion. NUC-05, Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors, concerns obtaining credible information about reactor operation; it is distinct from a spacecraft's own controls and from demonstrating successful payload delivery.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-01, A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant, and NUC-07, Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle, concern different energy-generation breakthroughs. A future fusion system might be considered for propulsion, but net electricity generation alone would not establish flightworthy mass, integrated propulsion or mission endurance. The concrete reactor and propulsion developments documented in this record concern the fission-based electric route.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-03, A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides, and NUC-13, A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance, address fuel-cycle outcomes rather than propulsion performance. Fuel selection and handling can intersect with spacecraft reactor design, but successful deep-space propulsion would not by itself demonstrate either actinide consumption at scale or stronger intrinsic proliferation resistance.

change_log.change: Preserved NUC-04's identity and broad nuclear propulsion scope while distinguishing nuclear thermal and nuclear electric architectures.
change_log.reason: The concept covers both routes, while the supplied technical evidence primarily supports discussion of the electric route.

change_log.change: Expanded the explanation of integrated spacecraft requirements, propulsion tradeoffs and mission-duration endurance.
change_log.reason: The review provides useful technical reasoning that separate component achievements and high electrical power do not establish mission capability.

change_log.change: Specified the 2018 KRUSTY result as a 28-hour full-power ground test with electrical conversion, without implying propulsion flight or ten-year tested endurance.
change_log.reason: The reviewed source distinguishes the demonstrated experiment from longer-term design capability.

change_log.change: Specified February 2026 testing, the April 28 article date and the thruster's reported input power of up to 120 kW.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the quantitative result while avoiding unsupported implications about thrust, reactor-powered operation or mission endurance.

change_log.change: Corrected October 20 from an established announcement-event date to the SR-1 article date, and retained the 2028 launch as a plan.
change_log.reason: The supplied review establishes the article date and future mission description, but does not date the referenced announcement event.

change_log.change: Preserved the SR-1 post-cutoff update limitation and the lack of a comprehensive freshness survey.
change_log.reason: The November 6 retained copy cannot establish exact November 1 wording or a comprehensive status assessment.

change_log.change: Qualified the historical nuclear thermal ground-test assertion instead of treating it as a documented milestone.
change_log.reason: The supplied reviewed texts do not substantiate that assertion; this is an evidence gap rather than proof that the history is false.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria operational through predefined payload, duration, comparison metrics, integrated measurements and subsequent flights.
change_log.reason: The review recommends testable mission-specific criteria while preserving their proposed nature and bounded applicability.

change_log.change: Added distinct relationships to every other supplied roster entry as explicitly labeled synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supports conceptual comparisons, but does not provide evidence that those separate innovations are achieved or mandatory prerequisites.

unresolved_issues: The exact pre-November 1, 2026 wording of the SR-1 article remains unrecovered; the retained copy was updated November 6.
The supplied material does not establish a comprehensive current-state survey as of the assessment cutoff.
Historical nuclear thermal engine ground-test antecedents remain unverified within the supplied reviewed evidence.
Mission-specific acceptable system mass, shielding, control requirements, endurance and reliability thresholds remain undefined.
No particular payload, trajectory, chemical comparator, cost boundary or number of repeat flights has been selected for the proposed completion demonstration.
